# Toolbar actions: a general showOnFocus observing containsFocus, replacing tab.Container's hand-rolled body-focus gate

Toolbar actions gate on `contextual: true`, a boolean that says an action *is* gated but never *by
what*. Reading it means chasing `toolbar.Base#contextualActionsVisible` into `tab.Container`'s three
hand-rolled focus handlers and then into `isBodyFocusPath`.

Three things follow, and the third is the reason this is worth doing rather than a rename.

## 1. The name is out of step with the engine's own vocabulary

`form.field.trigger.Base` already ships **`showOnHover`** — a per-item visibility trigger, defaulted
`true` on `CopyToClipboard`, consumed by `Clear`. The engine has a `showOnX` idiom for exactly this
concept; `contextual` is the odd one out, and a second name for one idea is a lookup every reader pays.

## 2. The gate is wired bespoke, so nothing but a TabContainer can use it

`contextualActionsVisible` has exactly one driver in the codebase — `tab/Container.mjs`, three
hand-rolled handlers. Any other toolbar setting `contextual: true` gets an action hidden **forever**,
because nothing drives its gate and the config defaults to `false`. A silent, permanently-absent
action is the worst available failure for a visibility feature: nothing errors, it simply never
appears.

Worse, the wiring re-derives from focus *events* what the framework already maintains as *state*.
`manager.Focus.setComponentFocus` keeps **`containsFocus`** — a reactive config on
`component.Base` — current on every component in the focus path. The gate is a subscription to
existing state, not a second interpretation of focus events.

## 3. Gating on the tab BODY is wrong, and it is the bug under the ugliness

`isBodyFocusPath` arms only when focus reaches the body container. That means **a tab whose body
holds nothing focusable can never expose its own header actions** — the actions exist, are correct,
and are unreachable. It also splits one concept across two edges (arm on body, disarm on the whole
container) purely to stop an action vanishing as the pointer reaches it.

The subject should be the **TabContainer**: focus anywhere inside it — a tab button, the body, one of
these actions — exposes the gated actions; only leaving hides them.

That also makes the two edges collapse into one subject, which is a property of `manager.Focus`
rather than a simplification: it fires focus transitions only up to the closest component common to
the old and new paths. Focus moving *within* the subject never clears the subject's own
`containsFocus`, so an action cannot vanish from under the pointer reaching for it — no arm/disarm
split required.

For a tab header toolbar the TabContainer is simply its **parent**, so the general default — observe
the parent — is exactly right, and `tab.Container` needs no focus code at all.

## Scope

- Add `showOnFocus` as the action-level config. Keep `contextual` working as a deprecated alias so
  the shipped consumers (`code/LivePreview.mjs`, `dashboard/dock/projection/LayoutAdapter.mjs`) are
  unaffected.
- Give `toolbar.Base` a `focusSubjectId` defaulting to its parent, and drive
  `contextualActionsVisible` by observing the subject's reactive `containsFocus` via `observeConfig`,
  which also ties the subscription to the toolbar's lifecycle.
- Delete `tab.Container`'s `onFocusEnter` / `onFocusMove` / `onFocusLeave` / `isBodyFocusPath`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] An action declares `showOnFocus: true` and is exposed while its toolbar's focus subject holds
      focus.
- [ ] The gate observes the subject's reactive `containsFocus` config; it does not re-derive focus
      state from `focusEnter` / `focusLeave` handlers.
- [ ] `contextual: true` keeps working as a deprecated alias, and an explicit opt-out in **either**
      spelling outranks `actionDefaults` — proven for a subclass whose defaults still use the old
      spelling, since the two keys otherwise both survive the config spread.
- [ ] A plain `toolbar.Base` with a `showOnFocus` action is exposed when its parent gains focus and
      hidden when the parent loses it — i.e. the capability works with no TabContainer involved.
- [ ] Focus moving from elsewhere in the subject **onto one of these actions** keeps them exposed,
      proven by an arm that fails if the subject is the body rather than the container.
- [ ] Focusing a tab button alone exposes the actions — the case body-gating got wrong.
- [ ] `tab.Container` no longer implements focus handlers or `isBodyFocusPath` for this purpose.

## Contract Ledger

Added 2026-08-30 at reviewer request (PR #17875 RA-2). This is the surface the implementation is held
to; the PR reconciles against these rows.

### Action-level gate

| key | type | status | contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `showOnFocus` | Boolean | **current** | `true` ⇒ the action is exposed only while its toolbar's focus subject holds focus. Named to match the engine's existing `showOnHover` on `form.field.trigger.Base`. |
| `contextual` | Boolean | **deprecated alias** | Accepted as INPUT only. It is resolved into `showOnFocus` and **deleted**; no instance ever carries both, so no reader reconciles two spellings. |

### Precedence — explicit, not positional

A config spread cannot express this: `showOnFocus` and `contextual` are different keys, so **both
survive it** and whichever deprecated value happened to be truthy would decide. Resolution is
therefore an ordered chain, nearest-first and current-name-before-alias:

| # | source | key |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the action's own config | `showOnFocus` |
| 2 | the action's own config | `contextual` |
| 3 | `actionDefaults` | `showOnFocus` |
| 4 | `actionDefaults` | `contextual` |
| — | none of the above | no gate key is set; the action is persistent |

Rows 3–4 are the case with no "own" value to prefer — a subclass whose `actionDefaults` carry **both**
keys. The current key decides there too, in both directions.

`tab.header.Toolbar` sets `actionDefaults: {showOnFocus: true}`, so a tab header action is gated
unless it opts out. The two shipped callers (`code/LivePreview.mjs`, `dashboard/dock/projection/LayoutAdapter.mjs`)
opt out with the deprecated spelling and stay persistent.

### Focus subject

| aspect | contract |
|---|---|
| `focusSubjectId` | Component whose focus exposes this toolbar's gated actions. `null` resolves to the toolbar's **parent** — for a tab header toolbar that is the TabContainer itself. |
| resolution timing | Idempotent and retried: attempted at the toolbar's `onConstructed` and again on mount, and by the owner once its children exist. A subject that cannot be resolved leaves the toolbar unwired rather than marked done. |
| both edges, one subject | `manager.Focus` fires transitions only up to the closest component common to the old and new paths. Focus moving anywhere INSIDE the subject — including onto one of these actions — never clears the subject's `containsFocus`, so an action cannot vanish from under the pointer reaching for it. Only leaving the subject re-hides them. |

### Visibility lifecycle

| aspect | contract |
|---|---|
| source of truth | The subject's reactive `containsFocus` config, consumed via `observeConfig()` — **not** re-derived from `focusEnter` / `focusLeave` handlers. The subscription is tied to the toolbar's lifecycle. |
| initial adoption | A subject already holding focus at wiring time is adopted once, because a subscription reports only changes. |
| `contextualActionsVisible` | Remains a public reactive config, so a composition whose exposing signal is not focus can still drive it directly. |
| hidden representation | `visibility: hidden` + `pointer-events: none`, plus `aria-hidden`, `inert`, `tabIndex: -1`. **Layout extent is preserved**, so arming and disarming never reflow the toolbar. Consumer-owned `hidden` and `disabled` state is untouched. |

## Out of Scope

- Adding extra actions to Dock-projected tab headers. `LayoutAdapter` builds `headerActions` only
  from its close action and forwards only the `close` intent; that seam is a separate leaf.
- Other trigger kinds (`showOnHover` for toolbar actions, selection- or edit-gated actions). The
  subject model leaves room for them; none is implemented here.
